title: The coat and the dreams (Genesis 37:1–11)
hook: a favorite son, a colored coat, and brothers who can't speak peaceably

segments.voice: Yesterday, meeting Esau: the wronged brother ran first. Your line was he ran to meet him. Did you take your small step toward someone? Today, the next generation, and the trouble starts again. Day three hundred sixty.

Some family photo albums have one: the kid in the middle of every picture. The one whose drawings went on the fridge, whose birthday got the bigger cake, who got away with things. A sibling can still name that kid, years later. Genesis has watched this pattern before. Isaac loved Esau more. Rebecca loved Jacob more. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah. And now Jacob, old, called Israel, has twelve sons, and he doesn't even try to hide which one is his favorite.
screen: `THE KID IN EVERY PICTURE.` → `A FAMILY OF FAVORITES.` → `TWELVE SONS, ONE FAVORITE.`

segments.voice: First, the favorite. Joseph is seventeen, the son of Rachel, the wife Jacob loved, born when Jacob was old. He tends the flocks with his older half-brothers and brings his father a bad report about them. Second, the coat. In the Douay-Rheims: "Now Israel loved Joseph above all his sons, because he had him in his old age: and he made him a coat of divers colours. And his brethren seeing that he was loved by his father, more than all his sons, hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him." Could not speak peaceably. Not even hello. Here's something honest about that coat: nobody is sure exactly what it looked like. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, gives it many colors. Some readers take the Hebrew phrase, ketonet passim, as a long robe, the kind the second book of Samuel says a king's daughters wore. Either way, it wasn't work clothes. It said: this one doesn't do what you do. Third, the dreams. Joseph dreams that his brothers' sheaves of grain bow down to his sheaf. Then that the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him. And he tells them. Both times. The brothers hate him more. Even his father rebukes him: are your mother and I and your brothers to bow down to you? Fourth, the quiet line. The brothers envied him, Genesis says, but his father kept the matter in mind. Catholics may hear an echo in Luke, where Mary keeps things and ponders them in her heart. A father who caused the trouble also senses something in it he can't yet see.
screen: `SEVENTEEN, AND THE FAVORITE.` · `A COAT THAT SAID: NOT LIKE YOU.` · `SHEAVES AND STARS BOW DOWN.` · `HIS FATHER KEPT THE MATTER.` · then, large: `COULD NOT SPEAK PEACEABLY TO HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice favoritism around you. Settle, and breathe. Think through the places you spend time: your family, your workplace, your parish, your group of friends. Where is someone treated as the favorite, and someone else as the afterthought? Don't rush to blame anyone. Just see it. Then look honestly at yourself: is there anyone you favor without meaning to, a child, a coworker, a friend? And anyone you overlook? If you pray, you can ask for a fairer heart. The bell holds the time.
The coat and the dreams. Jacob's special robe for his favorite son, and Joseph's dreams of his family bowing down: the start of the long Joseph story.
screen: `THE COAT AND THE DREAMS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the coat caused trouble. Today, give one person you usually overlook the kind of attention you usually save for your favorite. Day three hundred sixty.

howItsDone: The Church reads the Joseph story in the weekday Mass during Lent, setting the brothers' envy beside the plot against Jesus in the Gospel.

fork.setup: you're Joseph, seventeen. you've dreamed that your brothers' sheaves bowed down to yours. they already can't stand you. what do you do?
fork.reveal: he tells them, and then tells them a second dream too. they hate him more, and even his father rebukes him, though he keeps the matter in mind.

original.note: Hebrew: Joseph's coat. many colors in the Douay-Rheims; some read a long robe. the exact meaning is uncertain.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a colorful coat.
what it means: a father's open favoritism, a coat that says not like you, and brothers who can't even say hello.
what a scholar hears: ketonet passim is uncertain; the same phrase describes a king's daughter's robe in 2 Samuel 13.

sources.quoted: Now Israel loved Joseph above all his sons, because he had him in his old age: and he made him a coat of divers colours. And his brethren seeing that he was loved by his father, more than all his sons, hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 37:3–4 quoted from memory ('colours' is the translation's spelling inside the quotation); confirm wording.

Coat: Septuagint chitona poikilon, Vulgate tunicam polymitam (many colors); Hebrew ketonet passim possibly 'long-sleeved' or 'ankle-length'; same phrase in 2 Samuel 13:18 (Tamar). Confirm. The index's 'colored coat' is kept in the hook.

37:10 rebuke paraphrased; 37:11 'his father kept the matter in mind' paraphrased (Douay-Rheims: 'his father considered the thing with himself'). The Luke 2:19 echo is offered as something Catholics 'may hear', not as the text's intent. Confirm.
The outline's practice spelling 'favouritism' is written as 'favoritism' (American spelling).
howItsDone: Genesis 37:3–4, 12–13a, 17b–28 is read on Friday of the Second Week of Lent with the parable of the wicked tenants. Confirm.
